claims.text: Key takeaway and FAQ 'Is an EOB a bill?': an EOB is the plan's record of how a claim was processed, not a bill; the bill comes from the provider (also citable summary)
claims.quote: An explanation of benefits isn't a bill. It helps you understand how much your health plan covers, and what you'll pay when you get a bill from your provider.

claims.text: Parts table: patient, health plan, who provided care and when, claim number, payee for overpayments
claims.quote: You (the patient) Your health plan Who provided your care, and when it was provided A reference number called the claim number The person who gets reimbursed for any overpayments, called the payee

claims.text: Parts table and body: date of service and service description (visit, lab test)
claims.quote: The date of service A service description. This explains what service you had, like a medical visit, lab test, or screening.

claims.text: Parts table and body (rewritten): provider charges = amount billed; allowed charges = amount provider will be paid, may differ; paid by insurer = what plan pays provider
claims.quote: “Provider Charges” is the amount your provider bills for your visit. “Allowed Charges” is the amount your provider will be paid. This may not be the same as the Provider Charges.

claims.text: Body (rewritten), table and how-to step 3: what you owe / patient balance is what is left after insurer pays; EOB does not show whether you already paid part
claims.quote: What You Owe, or Patient Balance, is the amount you owe after your insurer has paid everything else. ... The Explanation of Benefits only shows what you owe, not if you've already paid for it.

claims.text: Key takeaway, sequence paragraph (rewritten), how-to step 5, sample key 4, 'What to do if wrong' (rewritten), FAQs on bill higher than EOB: bill should not be higher than patient balance; if it is, talk to the provider
claims.quote: Your bill should not be higher than the Patient Balance. If it is, talk to your provider.

claims.text: Remark code paragraph, how-to step 4 and sample key 5 (rewritten): a note from the plan, usually 2 or 3 letters and numbers, explaining costs, charges and paid amounts; described at bottom of EOB
claims.quote: A remark code is a note from the health plan that explains more about the costs, charges, and paid amounts for your visit. The code is usually 2 or 3 letters and numbers. Check the bottom

claims.text: 'What to do if wrong': call the plan's number on the EOB
claims.quote: It will also list your health plan's phone number. Call your health plan if you have questions about finding a provider or what services they cover.

claims.text: Itemized bill list item and FAQ (rewritten): if something does not look right, ask for an itemized list of charges

claims.text: 'What to do if wrong' (new sentence replacing uncited 'common sign of a billing or coding error'): make sure the bill is accurately calculated and owed before paying

claims.text: Remark code paragraph: if the plan denies a claim, the insurer must notify you in writing and explain why
claims.quote: Your health plan denies the claim: Your insurer must notify you in writing and explain why

claims.text: 'What to do if wrong' and denied-claim FAQ: file an internal appeal within 180 days (6 months) of the denial notice; if still denied, file for external review
claims.quote: You must file your internal appeal within 180 days (6 months) of receiving notice that your claim was denied. ... If your insurance company still denies your claim, you can file for an external review.

claims.text: FAQ 'Do I need to keep my EOBs?': keep copies of claim and denial information, including EOBs showing what was denied
claims.quote: Keep copies of all information related to your claim and the denial. ... The Explanation of Benefits forms or letters showing what payment or services were denied

claims.text: Remark code paragraph: under federal rules for group health plans and insurers, the denial reason must include the denial code and its meaning
claims.quote: The plan and issuer must ensure that the reason or reasons for the adverse benefit determination or final internal adverse benefit determination includes the denial code and its corresponding meaning

claims.text: Remark code paragraph: the notice must explain how to start an appeal
claims.quote: The plan and issuer must provide a description of available internal appeals and external review processes, including information regarding how to initiate an appeal.

claims.text: 'What to do if wrong': these federal appeal rules generally do not apply to grandfathered health plans
